content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has evaluated the potential of a three-drug regimen consisting of ivermectin, diethylcarbamazine, and albendazole (IDA) as an alternative to the current two-drug regimens (diethylcarbamazine and albendazole or ivermectin and albendazole). Additionally, the feasibility of biannual mass drug administration (MDA) using the current two-drug regimens and albendazole, instead of annual MDA, has been considered. The assessment of these alternative approaches included a detailed review of the problem's priority, the benefits and harms, the certainty and quality of the evidence, resource implications, equity, acceptability, and feasibility. Based on the evidence reviewed, recommendations for alternative regimens were formulated to address specific epidemiological and technical situations. These recommendations were reviewed by the WHO steering committee, guideline methodologists, the guideline development group, and peer reviewers before submission to the WHO Guidelines Review Committee. Lymphatic filariasis (LF) is a vector-borne neglected tropical disease caused by infection with the filarial parasites Wuchereria bancrofti, Brugia malayi, and Brugia timori. Adult worms reside in the human lymphatic system, where they produce thousands of microfilariae that circulate in the peripheral blood, coinciding with the biting activity of mosquito vectors. These microfilariae are ingested by mosquitoes during blood feeding, develop within the insect, and are transmitted to other human hosts when the infected mosquito bites again. Filarial infections may be asymptomatic or present with acute manifestations such as fever, localized swelling, tropical pulmonary eosinophilia syndrome, and lymphangitis. Chronic complications include lymphoedema (elephantiasis) of the limbs, scrotal damage in men (hydrocele), kidney damage (including chyluria), and damage to the lymphatic system. Approximately 1 billion people in 72 countries live in areas where LF is endemic, with at least 36 million individuals suffering from associated morbidity. The disease, while not fatal, is a leading cause of permanent and long-term disability globally, as ranked by WHO. The Global Programme to Eliminate Lymphatic Filariasis (GPELF), launched by WHO in 2000, employs a two-pronged strategy: (i) interrupting transmission through annual MDA targeting eligible populations and (ii) implementing morbidity management and disability prevention to alleviate suffering. Elimination of LF as a public health problem is defined as reducing infection levels to the point where transmission is no longer sustainable and ensuring the availability of a basic care package for managing lymphoedema and hydrocele. To stop MDA, measurable elimination thresholds must be demonstrated, including microfilaraemia prevalence of less than 1% or antigenaemia prevalence of less than 2% in sentinel and spot-check surveys, and incident infection rates below 1% or 2% during transmission assessment surveys (TAS). Documentation of these thresholds being met for at least four consecutive years after MDA discontinuation is required to validate elimination claims. WHO recommends annual MDA with diethylcarbamazine and albendazole (DA) in communities without onchocerciasis, annual MDA with ivermectin and albendazole (IA) in areas co-endemic for LF and onchocerciasis, and biannual albendazole in areas co-endemic for LF and loiasis where ivermectin has not been distributed. These regimens aim to reduce transmission rates and prevent progression from subclinical to clinical disease, yielding economic savings and enhanced productivity. Despite significant progress under GPELF, 42% of endemic countries still require MDA, and achieving global elimination by 2020 is no longer feasible with existing regimens. WHO has therefore evaluated alternative regimens, including IDA and biannual MDA, to realign national programs toward elimination targets. These recommendations are intended to provide endemic countries with options for alternative MDA regimens where warranted, focusing solely on LF MDA and not covering other public health interventions such as morbidity management, vector control, or health education. The effectiveness of MDA depends on achieving at least 65% epidemiological coverage, defined as the proportion of the total population ingesting the medicines during MDA. In areas with poor drug coverage or intense transmission, more than five MDA rounds may be required to reduce infection levels below elimination thresholds. Strong political will, donor support, and coordinated partnerships have been critical to the program's success, with over 7 billion treatments delivered to more than 850 million people. WHO emphasizes the importance of ensuring the highest attainable level of health for all people globally while respecting their dignity, equality, and diversity. Many individuals suffering from LF are socially marginalized and face discrimination and stigmatization, particularly those with visible hydrocele and lymphoedema. Decision-makers in endemic countries are urged to address these challenges and implement strategies to eliminate LF as a public health problem.
